title: Level 2 Biology — Genetic Variation and Change (2025)
subject: biology

questions.text:
Fancy mice (Mus musculus) are popular pets kept by breeders worldwide. They show a complete dominance inheritance pattern for coat colour and tail length. The allele for brown coat (B) is dominant to the allele for white coat (b). The allele for long tail (T) is dominant to the allele for short tail (t). The genes for coat colour and tail length are not genetically linked.

A breeder crossed a mouse homozygous for brown coat and long tail with a mouse homozygous for white coat and short tail.

State the genotype of the gametes produced by each parent, and state the genotype of the F1 generation.
questions.expectedAnswer: Parent 1 gametes: BT. Parent 2 gametes: bt. Genotype of F1: BbTt.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies gametes OR F1 genotype correctly.

questions.text: Construct a Punnett square to show the gametes of the F1 generation, and all of the possible genotypes of the F2 generation.
questions.expectedAnswer: F1 gametes: BT, Bt, bT, bt.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Punnett square completed with correct gametes for F2.

questions.text:
State the predicted phenotype ratio of the F2 generation produced by this cross.

The expected distribution is shown in the graph below.
questions.expectedAnswer: 9:3:3:1 — 9 brown long : 3 brown short : 3 white long : 1 white short.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Phenotype ratio (with correct appearance): 9 brown long : 3 brown short : 3 white long : 1 white short.

questions.text:
The budgerigar (Melopsittacus undulatus) is a small parakeet in which feather colour involves both linked and unlinked genes. When budgerigars heterozygous for wing pattern and body colour are crossed, the striped allele (S) is dominant over plain (s), and the green body allele (G) is dominant over blue body colour (g).

With this cross, the observed ratio is often:
7 striped green : 1 striped blue : 1 plain green : 7 plain blue

Discuss how genes located on the same chromosome can show both linked and unlinked characteristics, using the information provided for BOTH the fancy mouse and the budgerigar.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- how the processes of crossing over and segregation can influence the inheritance patterns of both linked and unlinked genes
- the effect of gene location on the observed phenotype ratios
- why the dihybrid heterozygous crosses for these identified traits produce such different ratios in these two species.
questions.expectedAnswer: Linked genes are located close together on the same chromosome and tend to be inherited together. Unlinked genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently. Crossing over during meiosis can separate linked genes, producing recombinant offspring at a lower frequency than expected from independent assortment.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved (A3-A4): Describes linked genes; unlinked genes; crossing over (accept annotated diagram); segregation. Merit (M5-M6): Explains how the process of crossing over influences the inheritance patterns of both linked and unlinked genes on the same chromosome; how the process of segregation influences inheritance patterns of both linked and unlinked genes; why the two species have different ratios. Excellence (E7-E8): Provides detailed discussion of the inheritance patterns of linked and unlinked genes with reference to the ratios in the source material for both species; the processes of crossing over and segregation, confidently linked to the observed ratios in each species.

questions.text:
The tuatara (Sphenodon punctatus) is a reptile endemic to Aotearoa New Zealand. It has cultural significance to many iwi, who regard it as a taonga.

Genetic studies and historical records indicate that tuatara populations were once found across both main islands. Habitat loss caused by deforestation and predation by introduced mammals isolated populations into distinct groups on offshore islands and a few protected mainland sites.

The Brothers Island population of tuatara is genetically distinct from other populations. Conservation efforts include predator-free sanctuaries and translocation programmes.

Genetic analyses have revealed that tuatara populations on different islands have become genetically distinct. The smallest island populations show markedly lower genetic diversity, with some alleles becoming fixed.

The graph below shows the genetic diversity (measured as heterozygosity) across different tuatara populations.

Discuss what factors may cause allele frequencies in the tuatara gene pool to change, using the information provided above.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- how the gene pool of the tuatara could be affected by migration between habitats AND by genetic drift
- how natural selection and mate selection may have influenced the two distinct phenotypes of larger olive-green and smaller darker-coloured tuatara.
questions.expectedAnswer: Allele frequency: how common an allele is in a population. Gene pool: all the alleles present in a population. Genetic drift: random changes in allele frequency, more significant in small populations. Migration (gene flow) introduces new alleles, increasing genetic diversity.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved (A3-A4): Describes allele frequency; gene pool; genetic drift; natural selection; identify any ONE selection pressure (predation, temperature, food supply, habitat); population bottleneck; founder effect. Merit (M5-M6): Explains migration; genetic drift (must have idea of allele frequency increasing/fixed OR decreasing/lost) (accept founder or bottleneck effect explained as an example of genetic drift); effect of migration/genetic drift on small isolated populations; natural selection/mate selection (must have idea of allele frequency increasing/fixed OR decreasing/lost); why larger olive-green tuatara might be more successful in warm food-rich habitats; why smaller darker tuatara might be more successful in cooler exposed habitats. Excellence (E7-E8): Provides detailed discussion of how migration and genetic drift changed allele frequencies in the tuatara gene pool; the selection pressures that drive natural selection, in reference to the tuatara, and how it led to the different phenotypes seen across New Zealand populations.

questions.text:
When performing kidney transplants, it is essential to match the tissue type of the donor and recipient as closely as possible. A mismatch can trigger immune rejection of the transplanted organ.

Tissue type in humans is largely controlled by multiple alleles at the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) gene complex. Several HLA genes each have many alleles, and some alleles show co-dominance — both alleles in a heterozygous individual are expressed on the cell surface.

HLA types:
| Phenotype (surface markers expressed) | Example Genotypes |
|---|---|
| HLA-A1 only | HLA-A1/HLA-A1 |
| HLA-A2 only | HLA-A2/HLA-A2 |
| Both HLA-A1 and HLA-A2 | HLA-A1/HLA-A2 |
| HLA-A3 only | HLA-A3/HLA-A3 |

Consider a family where:
Parent 1 (father): expresses both HLA-A1 and HLA-A2 (genotype HLA-A1/HLA-A2)
Parent 2 (mother): expresses both HLA-A2 and HLA-A3 (genotype HLA-A2/HLA-A3)
Child 1 (son): expresses HLA-A2 only
Child 2 (daughter): expresses both HLA-A1 and HLA-A3

Discuss the inheritance of HLA types in this family, using the information provided above. You may include a Punnett square to support your answer (optional).

In your answer, include discussion of:
- what is meant by the term multiple alleles
- the possible genotypes of Child 1
- the difference between dominant alleles and co-dominant alleles
- how to determine the genotype of Child 1 by examining the HLA types of his future children, if his partner has the genotype HLA-A3/HLA-A3
- why such a determination of Child 1's genotype from his children's HLA types may not be guaranteed as accurate.
questions.expectedAnswer: Multiple alleles: more than two alleles exist for a single gene at the same locus in a population. Child 1 expresses HLA-A2 only, so possible genotypes are HLA-A2/HLA-A2 (one A2 from each parent). Co-dominant alleles are both expressed when present together.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved (A3-A4): Describes multiple alleles; the possible genotypes of the parents; the possible genotypes of Child 1 OR a monohybrid Punnett square showing possible genotypes of Child 1; complete dominance; co-dominance; possible phenotypes OR genotypes of the offspring of Child 1 with an HLA-A3/HLA-A3 partner OR provides a Punnett square. Merit (M5-M6): Explains why Child 1 has a specific genotype (must mention alleles of gametes from BOTH parents); complete dominance with an example; co-dominance with an HLA allele example; how to use offspring phenotypes to deduce Child 1's genotype (must mention alleles of gametes from BOTH parents). Excellence (E7-E8): Provides detailed discussion linking the idea of co-dominance and complete dominance to discuss the genotype of Child 1, based on the parents' genotypes and phenotypes; of the possibility to determine the genotype of Child 1, based on the HLA types of his children, if his partner was HLA-A3/HLA-A3, and why such a determination cannot be guaranteed to be correct (must use parental gametes and offspring genotypes with ratios/percentages).
